Discussion: An Agnostic Viewpoint on Multiple Personality Disorder

Donald Ross MD

Donald Ross

6501 North Charles Street
Baltimore, MD 21204

Donald Ross  

Multiple personality disorder has reemerged in psychiatry and has brought along a multiplicity of perplexing issues. I deeply appreciate Dr. Lyon's presenting such a marvelous case. Dr. Lyon immersed herself in the therapeutic task, tolerated and used her countertransference, struggled with the confusing aspects of the case, in short—made a heroic effort. If the therapeutic result was disappointing and we are left with many questions, Dr. Lyon's report is so clear and well articulated that it provides us with a great deal of valuable material for discussion.

Believers, Nonbelievers, and Agnostics

I shall be discussing this case from an agnostic viewpoint. What I mean is I am not going to use the case as a vehicle to illustrate certain principles I already know and understand. Rather, I am going to look at it to see what we can learn from the patient and her treatment. To call this an “agnostic viewpoint” may seem inappropriate. After all, we are referring to the clinical science of psychiatry, not religion. Unfortunately, one of the most vexing issues surrounding MPD is just this: that within psychiatry, there are camps of true believers and nonbelievers in MPD. Each has its own agenda, and neither really wants to hear the other's point of view.

Epilogue

Owen Renik Issue Editor

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

Our contributors have provided us with a very full discussion of the questions “What is interpretation?” and “What are its consequences?”. Every paper reflects clinical interest and experience on the author's part; there is no empty theorizing disconnected from observations made in the treatment situation. These are all clinical analysts, trying to understand how therapy really works. Yet, despite this important common ground, there is a striking lack of consensus with respect to the answers given to the questions posed.

The lack of agreement testifies to the fact that psychoanalytic science is still in an early stage of development. We struggle to realiably describe even the most fundamental aspects of an analyst's activity. No surprise, then, that the mechanism of action of analytic treatment and criteria for assessing effective analytic technique remain elusive for the moment.

Perhaps the term interpretation itself has become something of a burden. It certainly originated in a conception of the analytic enterprise that is now obsolete — one that viewed the analyst as a decoder of encrypted messages from the unconscious — and brings with it a confusing legacy. Intervention, used by most non-English-speaking analysts, seems much more to the point.

No matter what words we choose, however, we need to address certain ambiguities that limit our understanding of the analyst's activity and its role in the analytic process. The familiar question of whether suggestion is an aspect of analytic technique, mentioned in the prologue, is one issue.

Editorial Note

Joseph Lichtenberg Editor-in-Chief

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

We are proud to welcome as consulting editors a distinguished group of colleagues from abroad: Christopher Bollas, Andre Haynal, Lotte Kohler, Peter Kutter, Arnaldo Novelletto, Pinchas Noy, and Gunnar Windahl. We welcome also Leon Wurmser, who will serve as Liaison Editor.

Since the inception of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, we have sought contributions from the widest range of authors in and out of the United States. In our Tenth Anniversary Issue, we surveyed the development of psychoanalysis in the decade of the 80s in a number of countries. Gradually our readership has increased in Europe, and our new editors, as friends, contributors, and active supporters, will help us further to fulfill our mission “to contribute to and participate in the open-ended discourse that we believe constitutes the essence of a broad, encompassing, psychoanalytic inquiry” (as stated in our Credo).

Prologue

Andrew Schwartz Issue Editor

Andrew Schwartz

Andrew Schwartz  

Some 14 years ago now, a preeminent neuroscientist with a longstanding interest in psychoanalysis and derivative psychotherapies reopened in rather dramatic fashion a line of inquiry that Freud early on (1895) had envisioned, explored, but then abandoned as premature. In a 1978 lecture to a Harvard audience, Eric R. Kandel (1979) suggested that because of advances in basic research the time had perhaps arrived to begin again to sketch connections between data relating to information-dependent neural plasticity and the cellular neurobiology of learning, on the one hand, and, on the other, clinical findings about the origin of and the psychological treatment of neurosis and character disorder.

Since the time of Kandel's first formal steps toward interdisciplinary integration, the psychiatric and psychoanalytic literatures have expanded to include many additional attempts to meld insights from laboratory and consulting room. The five essays in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry both review the progress to date and, more relevantly, continue to show how data and concepts from cellular neurobiology, experimental psychology, ethology, and cognitive science may illuminate long-familiar clinical phenomena and observations.

More specifically, David Cooper traces the explicit and implicit role associating learning concepts have had in the theories and procedural recommendations of analysts from Freud onward.

Epilogue

Andrew Schwartz Issue Editor

Andrew Schwartz

Andrew Schwartz  

As gilbert long ago concluded, “Things are seldom what they seem,” and one might in attempting a summary of this volume note, even underscore, an intriguing present-day irony. Despite its political, academic, and economic ascendancy, “biological psychiatry” has yet to furnish us with data describing decisively the etiology, pathophysiology, and eradication of a single diagnostic entity (cf. Gold et al., 1988a, b). On the other hand, converging lines of evidence and derivative models from the laboratories of some the world's leading bench neuroscientists hold the now very real promise of explaining the basic nature, cause, and cure of “psychic conflict” and the character disorders it engenders.

More explicitly, current ideas and data from neurobiology, experimental psychology, and ethology can help us achieve three different but closely related objectives — first, the reconceptualization and even the laboratory investigation of such clinical and theoretical keystones as motivational processes, consciousness, and “the unconscious,” tasks which Hadley, Olds, and Wexler respectively undertake; second, the systematic and biologically sound reformulation of our understanding of symptom formation and therapeutic effect, ends to which Cooper contributes in his exploration of links between the fields of associative learning and psychoanalysis; and, finally, the placing of analytic technique on a solidly scientific foundation, a goal that Schwartz attempts to approach in his examination of affect, nonverbal communication, and determination of interpretive focus and timing.

Epilogue

Irene Chiarandini Issue Editor and Rogelio Sosnik Issue Editor

Rogelio Sosnik

Rogelio Sosnik  

The preceding papers have offered us the opportunity to reflect on various dimensions of the interrelation between psychoanalysis and ethical issues. We were offered new areas for reflection as we struggled to reconceptualize, to reconsider our positions via-à-vis social pathology and its consequences.

Our contributors have led us in the exploration of subjects that have occupied psychoanalysis since its founder understood how the culture is embedded in the psyche, as he also envisioned an educational and social role for the method he created, with the implied ethical questions thereby posed.

During World War II and soon afterward in Britain, analysts from the continent—Vienna, Berlin, Budapest—and their British colleagues dedicated much thought and effort to the development of therapeutic nurseries, to the application of psychoanalytic principles to health systems, to education, and to “prevention.” Perhaps at a time when a world that had existed (and had been taken for granted) was in ruins, those pioneers had not much time for theoretical reflections that linked their idealism to action. They affected their society in ways that now seem extraordinary and exemplary. In contrast, since then, psychoanalysts in most of the world seem to have retreated into their offices and institutions, while the world that seemed in ruins was rebuilt but not recovered.

We have seen distinct lines emerge in the course of our reading: our contributors enlarged the focus of the here-and-now to include the social context.

612

Experimental Studies of Higher Cortical Functions That Proceed Without Conscious Awareness

Bruce Wexler MD

Bruce Wexler

34 Park St.
New Haven, CT 06519

Bruce Wexler  

From a neuroscience perspective, it is usually assumed that many higher cortical functions proceed without conscious awareness. In a recent overview paper in Science, Kihlstrom (1987) presented data from multiple sources that demonstrate that this is true for human beings as well as for other animals. From this perspective, consciousness, rather than unconscious mental life, is more the exception and the mystery. It is only from the perspective of the conscious subjective self, and a science based on that self in ways and to an extent that it is often unaware, that unconscious processes have been deemed unusual and mysterious.

The experimental study of unconscious cortical processes, however, has proved difficult and controversial despite their apparent ubiquity. The difficulty has centered on the problem of demonstrating that experimental stimuli are indeed processed without conscious awareness. Several laboratory methods have been created for this purpose, subjected to close critical scrutiny (cf. Eriksen, 1960; Holender, 1986) and then modified in response to the criticisms. This process, extending across nearly 40 years, has led to the development of methods that at least in recent years have enabled laboratory scientists to study unconscious cortical processes with confidence and rigor.

Dr. Wexler is Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine.

David Cooper PHD

David Cooper

Chestnut Lodge
500 West Montgomery Ave.
Rockville, MD 20850

David Cooper  

Neural foundations of learning are being discovered, with far-reaching ramifications for cognitive science (Kandel, 1983; Schwartz, 1987, 1988; Rescorla, 1988; Alkon, 1989). This work establishes the importance of associative learning, a phenomenon that is of much potential interest to psychoanalysts, who, after all, attempt to learn about patients via their “free associations.” The neurophysiologists' work supports the ubiquity of Pavlovian or classical conditioning in the acquisition and activation of learning in various species, including humans. Psychoanalysts may welcome these developments, for if, as I will attempt to show, psychoanalytic practice is compatible with classical conditioning theory, we may be within view of a time when, as envisioned by Freud, neural correlates of psychoanalytic hypotheses can be established (for efforts in this direction, see Meyersburg & Post, 1979; Reiser, 1984; Schwartz, 1987, 1988). Whether one gravitates toward a positivistic or a hermeneutic view of the science of psychoanalysis, it seems desirable to establish that one's view of how the mind works does not violate knowledge gained from brain science of how the brain works.

Dr. Cooper is Director of Group Psychotherapy, Chestnut Lodge; he is a Candidate, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

A shorter version of this paper was presented at the annual meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association, May 1990. The author is grateful for the helpful discussions by Lynn Whisnant Reiser and Allan D. Rosenblatt.

The Psychotherapy of Multiple Personality Disorder: A Case Study

David Fink MD

David Fink

David Fink  

During the past decade, there has been a growing recognition of posttraumatic psychopathology (Terr, 1991). The relationship between early severe psychological trauma and dissociative disorders has been firmly established (Spiegel, 1984, 1990). The identification of posttraumatic syndromes in general, and dissociative disorders in particular, has been on the rise (Kluft, 1984; Putnam et al., 1986). As a result, interest in the treatment of these conditions has been reawakened. To date, however, there have been very few analytically oriented case studies that review the treatment of individuals with the most severe dissociative disturbance, multiple personality disorder (Marmer, 1980a, b; Berman, 1981).

It is the purpose of this paper to describe the clinical presentation and inpatient treatment of a patient with multiple personality disorder in order to highlight the characteristic clinical features and the primary psychotherapeutic concerns. Particular attention will be paid to the complex dissociative mechanisms employed in response to early psychological trauma. In this regard, the posttraumatic origins and defensive functions of alternate personalities will be explored.

Dr. Fink is Associate Director, Dissociative Disorders Program, Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital.

Epilogue

Donald Ross MD and Richard Loewenstein Issue Editors

Richard Loewenstein

Richard Loewenstein  

Multiple personalty and psychoanalysis are facing each other again after a century. Are they destined to be incompatible and remain separate? We hope not. Can a rapprochment be achieved which might enrich our understanding of dissociative phenomena and mental functioning in general? We are of the opinion that a report such as this is a first step in that direction.

In the opening article, we tried to identify and discuss the relationship between modern trauma theory, the clinical phenomena of MPD, and psychoanalytic theory. The role of a major paradigm shift and the attendent confusion and “factionalization” that results are especially emphasized in that discussion. Adherents to one paradigm may simply “see” a different world than aherents to a different paradigm. Although trauma theory and psychoanalytic theory may be different paradigms, we believe there is sufficient overlap to allow serious students of MPD to benefit from immersion in both worlds.

The two cases nicely illustrated the phenomena under discussion. Dr. Fink's case is cleaner and more polished, seen by the therapist throughout the course of treatment predominately from the modern trauma theory perspective. Dr. Lyon's case is abundantly rich in material that illustrates the dilemmas facing most psychoanalytically oriented practitioners who attempt to begin treating MPD patients. Her willingness to share her experience, including the countertransference phenomena, allows us to take this difficult step vicariously. Together the two cases bring to life the clash of the paradigms and highlight the opportunities for mutual enrichment for trauma theory and psychoanalytic theory.

172

The Role of Interpretation

Joseph Weiss MD

Joseph Weiss

2420 Sutter Street
San Francisco, CA 94115

Joseph Weiss  

My thesis here is that interpretation is useful to the extent that it contributes to the patient's working to disprove the unconscious beliefs that underlie his psychopathology. These beliefs are grim and maladaptive. They warn the patient that if he pursues certain normal, desirable goals he will put himself in danger. Therefore they hinder him in the pursuit of these goals. For example, the male's unconscious belief in castration as a punishment may impede him in the pursuit of a good sexual relationship. Interpretation helps the patient to gain insight into the maladaptive beliefs and the forbidden goals, thereby facilitating his working to disprove the beliefs and pursue the goals.

The ideas summarized above are part of a psychoanalytic theory of the mind, psychopathology, and therapy that I developed and that the Mt. Zion Psychotherapy Research Group, which I codirect with Harold Sampson, has been investigating for the last 20 years (Weiss et al., 1986). The Mt. Zion Group carries out its studies by formal quantitative methods, using the transcripts of psychoanalyses and psychoanalytic psychotherapies. It has completed several investigations on how interpretation influences the patient, which will be discussed below (Castan, in Weiss et al 1986; Bush and Gassner, in Weiss et al 1986; Fretter, 1984, Broitman, 1985; Norville, 1990). The findings support our theory and throw light on the role of interpretation.

Dr. Weiss is a Training Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute and Co-Director, San Francisco Psychotherapy Research Group.

There was a reason for my choosing as the title of my book not The Dream but The Interpretation of Dreams. Freud, 1925, p. 46

Interpretation has been at the center of psychoanalysis from its beginnings, but it has also evolved as the analytic enterprise has evolved. So it will hardly surprise anyone familiar with the shifts in stance and in perspective that have characterized the development of psychoanalysis that interpretation should itself require some sort of interpretation. What is interpretation? How is it generated, how delivered? What is its content, its scope, its aim, its authority? How does it influence the patient? These questions, among others, regularly occupy the interest of those who have taken up the topic (e.g., Ferenczi, 1928; Freud, 1933; Hartmann, 1951; E. Kris, 1951; Loewenstein, 1951; Gray, 1973, 1987; Arlow, 1979, 1987; Blum, 1983; Spence, 1982, 1986).

Formulation of psychoanalytic concepts and observations from the viewpoint of the method of free association offers an opportunity for reconsideration of these questions. I shall rely upon the distinction between interpretation as a continuing activity and interpretation as a particular kind of analytic intervention.

Ethics and Shame in the Countertransference

Silvia Sas MD

Silvia Sas

40 Chemin des Coudriers
1209 Geneva
Switzerland

Silvia Sas  

In the therapeutic process with patients that have suffered from man-made extreme situations, the psychoanalyst experiences extreme ethical dilemmas somehow similar to the ones the patient faces. The therapeutic task implies the elaboration and transformation of these dilemmas in internal conflicts of values and meanings that may reestablish the possibility of ethical choices. The therapist questions himself about the “how” and “what” of his interpretations, but most particularly, at an existential level, the “what for” and even the “why me.” The ethical risk for the therapist is to collude (without awareness) with the torturing system that has been incorporated by the patient and occupies his or her inner life and actually permeates or imprints the therapeutical situation. This “imprinting” or “occupation” has been obtained by the torturing system through the immersion of the victim in a world of fraud and perversion to which he has been obliged to adapt, or, in other words: to get “accustomed to.”

Thinking about countertransference, it is important to acknowledge the penetrability of the phenomena manipulated by man-made social terror, even far away (in time and space) from the traumatic situation. The dismantling of values and symbolic thought may insidiously manifest itself inside the protected therapeutic setting.

Dr. Amati Sas is Training and Supervising Analyst, Swiss Psychoanalytic Society.

Richard Kluft MD

Multiple personality disorder (MPD) is a complex and chronic dissociative disorder involving difficulties in the integration of memory and identity (Nemiah, 1980; Kluft, 1987a). It is currently understood to be a sequel of overwhelming childhood experiences (Kluft, 1987a; Putnam, 1989). Few if any mental disorders are surrounded with such controversy and evoke such highly polarized and tenaciously maintained opinions in otherwise circumspect and scrupulous clinicians and scientific investigators (Goodwin, 1985; Kluft, 1985). Few mental disorders, apart from the organic mental syndromes, have remained as remote from the mainstream of contemporary psychoanalytic inquiry as has MPD (Kluft, 1989).

There is a certain historical irony to this, because Anna O., the index patient of the seminal “Studies on Hysteria” (Breuer & Freud, 1893-1895), suffered this disorder. Jones (1953), Freud's preeminent biographer, noted that Anna O. had “two distinct states of consciousness … rather like that in Morton Prince's famous case of Sally Beauchamp. It was a case of double personality. The transition from one to the other was marked by a phase of autohypnosis” (p. 223).

Dr. Kluft is Director of the Dissociative Disorders Program, The Institute of Pennsylvania Hospital; he is also Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Temple University School of Medicine.

Frank Putnam  

One of the finest academic traditions of medicine is the clinical case conference. Customarily a resident shares clinical material which is then sagely discussed by a visiting graybeard who attempts to provide insight into the pathological processes, offer treatment recommendations, share some thoughts about the prognosis, and venture some generalizations about the disorder. All parties hope he or she will also impart a larger perspective or theoretical position that serves to organize the case and generate a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics. One of the strengths of such conferences is that the discussants are specifically asked to focus on precisely this last task, the imparting of a clinical perspective, theoretical position, or dynamic model that can be applied to other cases.

It is the challenge of demonstrating that one's model or position is applicable, relevant, and useful that each discussant faces today as we come to grips the clinical material presented here. Dr. Lyon has provided us with a richly detailed and evocative case, including her own responses and her attempts to understand and utilize them in the treatment of this very difficult patient. Her metaphor, the shattered mirror, conveys a powerful image of what appears to have gone wrong and evokes a bleak picture of the patient's ultimate prognosis.

Dr. Putnam is Chief of the Unit on Dissociative Disorders, Laboratory of Developmental Psychology, National Institute of Mental Health.

It has always been Difficult for analysts to agree about the specific elements in psychoanalysis that are responsible for psychic change. Although “making the unconscious conscious” and “experiential knowledge” rather than just intellectual understanding are considered necessary, disagreement still exists over how the analytic experience leads to psychic change.

Interpretations are an essential technical tool in psychoanalysis; by exposing conflictual elements within the patient, enhancing the patient's simulataneous observation and experiencing of his psychic structure at work, and calling his attention to aspects of important relationships (past and present, real and fantasized), as they emerge in the transference, they make a major contribution to the development of insight. What remains elusive and difficult to substantiate is the link between interpretations, the development of insight, and change in psychic functioning, as well as where in the analytic process the change occurs. What to interpret, when to interpret, how to make the awareness of previously unconscious wishes and fantasies truly useful — these are subtle technical questions for which there is no single answer. But not only is there no set answer for these technical questions, the more fundamental question of the value and role of interpretations is also unresolved.

Dr. Chused is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute, Clinical Professor of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and Clinical Professor of Pediatrics at George Washington University School of Medicine.

On Pluralism in Psychoanalysis

Ricardo Bernardi MD

Ricardo Bernardi

Santiago Vazquez 1142

Ricardo Bernardi  

Psychoanalysis today is no longer defined by a central unifying theory that distinguishes it from all other psychologies. On the contrary, contemporary psychoanalytic thinking forces upon us the awareness of the many different theories that have evolved within our field. This development leads me to reflect on many different questions: How can we analysts turn our diversity to an advantage? How to solve the problem of each approach's proclaiming its own scientific value above the others? How is the individual analyst affected by this diversity in his own ideals pertaining to truth, knowledge, and validity? And how much tolerance are we psychoanalysts capable of?

In my attempt to answer these questions a number of epistemological and ethical factors emerge. I have attempted a definite psychoanalytic approach to these essentially ethical questions. When faced with the problem of pluralism in psychoanalysis, my approach aims to provide a better understanding of the mechanisms involved in both the acknowledgment or rejection of the other's point of view.

I begin with a systematic study of these aspects as they appear in contemporary practice.

The problem of pluralism in current psychoanalysis was posed by Wallerstein (1988)

Review of the Literature

Jim Dimon MD

Jim Dimon

2116 Sutter Street
San Francisco, CA 94115

Jim Dimon  

The varied psychoanalytic understandings of interpretation are foreshadowed by the diverse preanalytic meanings of the term. An interpreter, for example, is a translator from one language to another, an artist who gives creative meaning to a work of art, a scientist who accounts for a body of data, or a religious figure who reveals the will of God. Each of these usages is analogous to a psychoanalytic theory of interpretation.

Psychoanalytic thinking about interpretation has necessarily developed in conjunction with the evolution of related ideas. Interpretation is inevitably connected to theories of psychopathology (what is to be interpreted) and theories of therapeutic action (how interpretation works). The pluralism of psychoanalytic thought consequently applies to the concept of interpretation, and to examine the literature on this subject is to encounter controversies, past and present.

Freud began with a choice. He first used the word we translate as “interpretation” in a title, “The Interpretation of Dreams” (1900). He chose the German word Deutung, which in common usage referred to seers, who read the future from signs — including dreams. He conspicuously did not choose the word Erklaeren, used by scientific contemporaries to describe their explanations of things. As we know, Freud was more in accord with the popular view that dreams are meaningful than with the “scientific” conception then current of dreams as purely physiological events.

Dr. Dimon is a member of the Faculty of the San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute.

Samuel Abrams MD

Samuel Abrams

25 East 83rd Street
New York, NY 10028

Samuel Abrams  

In recent years, you've written a good deal about ambiguities in psychoanalysis and how they obstruct the work. Is “interpretation” also one of those ambiguous words?

I've written that an excess of ambiguities obstructs both clinical work and advances in our discipline at large. As a matter of fact, a certain degree of ambiguity is useful. It allows data that we haven't entirely yet understood to be gathered in for further study, data that might otherwise be passed over. A science that neglects what is does not yet understand is sterile. Interpretation is one of our appropriate ambiguities, although perhaps by now it too is bordering on excess.

How would you define interpretation?

I'd prefer to outline descriptive categories for study rather than merely offer a definition. For example, I suspect that you would be interested in the context or the climate of interpretations.

I would imagine that the content would be more interesting.

The context is as important as the content, and both shape the intent of the interpretation.

Discussion: A Psychoanalyst's Perspective on Multiple Personality Disorder

Sheldon Roth MD

Sheldon Roth

1765 Beacon Street
Newton, MA 02168

Sheldon Roth  

It was in the writings of Harry Stack Sullivan that I gained my first empathic appreciation of schizophrenia. Sullivan (1953a, pp. 331-339) conjured up the early-morning awakening from a disturbing dream whose mood refused to loosen its grip upon one's sense. Half-responsive to the realistic demands of another morning, and half-beckoned by the siren mood of the dream, we move about, semifrozen, perplexed citizens of two disparate worlds. Extending this example of Sullivan's view that “we are [all] much more human than otherwise” (1953b, p. 16), I ask you to consider that each night, in dreams, we experience the world of multiple personality. And, in the morning, like the host personality of a “multiple,” we have partial or total amnesia for our complex noctural alter activities.

Trauma is common to the etiology of both dreams and multiple personality. Freud's dream theory relied on a model of traumatic dissociation. A daytime experience (Freud's “day residue”), stimulates impulses that threaten psychological safety and are put beyond the reach of waking consciousness. Later, during dreaming sleep, the ego is flooded with visual flashbacks, hallucinatory, dramatized attempts to gratify the forbidden impulses of the day.

Dr. Roth is Training and Supervising Analyst at the Psychoanalytic Institute of New England, East; he is also Clinical Instructor in Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School.

Interpretive Sequence

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 Eighteenth Street, NW
Washington, DC 20009

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Psychoanalysis involves a unique, affective-cognitive, verbal and nonverbal interaction between analysand and analyst. Because the goal is to explore the intrapsychic realm of the analysand, most studies of the analytic process give primary attention to the analysand's associations as the fundamental source of information. I propose to reverse the usual focus from the analysand's communications to the analyst's interventions. My focus shifts not simply to one or more interpretations that are studied for evidence of the analyst's understanding or style or theoretical stance but to a sequence of interpretations. By sequence of interpretations I mean the interventions the analyst makes or does not make in a unit of time; in the example to follow, in one week of analysis. Ideally through the sequence of interpretations, the analyst conveys a coherence sense of purpose enabling the successive interventions to have a cumulative effect. I hope to demonstrate that the sequence of interpretations constitutes in the aggregate a substantial component of the work toward understanding and change that takes place in a successful analysis.

Attention centered on either the analysand's associations or the analyst's interventions does violence to the unity of the two-person experience. Appropriately we take as our usual position that the analyst's interventions are responses to the analysand's communications guided by the analyst's comprehension of their meaning.

Dr. Lichtenberg is Editor-in-Chief of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at Georgetown University.

The Instincts Revisited

June Hadley MD

June Hadley

3158 Booth Heights Road
East Troy, WI 53120

June Hadley  

When freud (1915) placed the instincts “on the frontier between the mental and the somatic” (p. 122) he anticipated our present endeavor to address the interface of psychoanalysis and neuroscience. His view of an instinct was that of an endogenous excitation or “stimulus applied to the mind”; he noted its constant effects as opposed to external stimuli which are “momentary” (p. 118). He made the assumption that “the nervous system is an apparatus which has the function of getting rid of the stimuli that reach it, or of reducing them to the lowest possible level; or which, if it were feasible, would maintain itself in an altogether unstimulated condition” (p. 120).

Freud later (1920), in “Beyond the Pleasure Principle,” amended this view as follows: “The mental apparatus endeavours to keep the quantity of excitation present in it as low as possible or at least to keep it constant” (p. 9, emphasis added). He used the term “Nirvana principle” to denote that condition and saw it as distinct from the “pleasure principle.” He viewed the pleasure principle as a transformation by libido or “life instinct” of the Nirvana principle, which he aligned with the “death instinct.”

In “Instincts and their Vicissitudes” Freud proposes two groups of primal instincts: “the ego, or self-preservative instincts and the sexual instincts” (p. 124).

Dr. Hadley is in the private practice of adult and child psychiatry; she has written extensively about the interface of neuroscience and psychoanalysis.

Belonging and Ethics

Janine Puget MD

Janine Puget

Paraguay 2465 po 7
1121 Buenos Aires
Argentina

Janine Puget  

This paper is prompted by reflections on the challenges posed to analysts who are working in situations of social catastrophe or social violence. Such situations induce particular moral distortions, the analyst, faced with such distortions — a pervasive deterioration of values and a confusion of ethical standards — may experience a particular kind of dilemma. The analytic focus has to be enlarged to permit interpretations that consider ethical issues as well as instinctual conflict.

In this paper I deal with that ethical aspect, taking into account the rules and values that regulate the subject's relations to his social milieu and his family (Puget, 1991), with special emphasis on the need to belong.

I start from the assumption that ethical issues appear as a struggle against irrationality by means of impositions and guilt as a regulatory feeling. In this context guilt is related to moral conscience and to responsibility; more specifically to neighborly love and value judgments.

Psychoanalytic practice confronts us with the difficulties inherent to a discipline that has as one of its tasks that of giving meaning to the irrational.

Dr. Puget is Training and Supervising Analyst in the Asociación Psicoanalítica de Buenos Aires (A.P.de B.A.). She is also Director of Research in Couple Psychoanalysis in the Asociación Argentina de Psicología y Psicoterapia de Grupo (A.A.P.P.de G.).

Consciousness: A Brain-Centered, Informational Approach

David Olds MD

David Olds

2211 Broadway, 1H
New York, N.Y. 10024

David Olds  

This paper is the second in a series exploring the nature of a brain-centered psychology. In the first paper (Olds, 1990) I developed the idea of a psychology that would consider the brain as its central organizing concept, in lieu of previous abstractions such as ego, id, or internal objects. The rationale for this change is to organize all of our thinking about mental agencies, mental process, and psychological function in general with reference to brain processes. The goal of such a psychology, not fully realizable as yet, is to ground all mental processes in biology in a manner resembling that of Freud's early hopes. The model is an information-processing one, in which information and semiotic functions serve to bridge the gap between brain and mind.

I here pursue this idea further in discussing the phenomenon of consciousness. Once this model is developed I will try to show that such a model places the psychoanalytic concepts of the unconscious and of psychoanalytic therapy in a different light, bringing them into line with current research in brain function and biology. The ultimate aim of such an endeavor is to ground psychoanalytic theory in a currently relevant scientific context.

Writing about consciousness is a kind of quicksand.

Dr. Olds is Training and Supervising Analyst, The Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

Prologue

Owen Renik Issue Editor

Owen Renik

Owen Renik  

The participants in this issue of Psychoanaltyic Inquiry, by agreeing to address the topic of interpretation and its consequences, have implicitly taken on the formidable task of discussing analytic process in relation to analytic technique—i.e., they are willing to say what they think actually takes place when a clinical analysis is successful and what role the analyst's activity plays in the sequence of events. This is perhaps something that every practicing analyst should be willing and able to do, but the fact is that relatively few do it. The whole question of how analysis works is regarded as notoriously elusive; and we tend to teach the practice of clinical analysis by example, in supervision, rather than with direct reference to systematic theory.

In the literature review that sets the stage for our symposium Jim Dimon outlines the complex implications of the topic. Common usage casts the interpreter in multiple roles: translator, creator, scientist, religious exigete. Dimon shows that each of these colloquial views corresponds to a trend within analytic theory, and he traces the thread of each trend through selections not only from what has been written about interpretation per se, but from the literature on psychopathology, therapeutic action, child treatment, and a variety of other relevant analytic subjects.

Each of the contributors to our symposium has a well-developed conception of analytic process, is able to articulate it, and brings it to bear in discussing technique.

We shall not cease from exploration

And the end of all our exploring

Will be to arrive where we started

And know the place for the first time.

T.S. Eliot, “Little Gidding”

Psychoanalytic concepts and techniques, in order to retain their vitality, must again and again be discovered by the analyst as if for the first time. The analyst must allow himself to be freshly surprised by the ideas and phenomena that he takes most for granted. For example, he must be able to allow himself to be genuinely caught off guard by the pervasiveness of the influence of the unconscious mind, by the power of the transference, and by the intrasigence of resistance, and only retrospectively apply the familiar names to these freshly rediscovered phenomena. If the analyst allows himself perpetually to be the beginner that he is, it is sometimes possible to learn about that which he thought he already knew. The present paper is a collection of thoughts addressed to myself (and other novices)

From Authoritarian Discourse to Psychoanalytic Discourse: A Psychoanalytic View of Ethics

Delia Faigon MD and Maria Siquier MD

Maria Siquier

Las Heras 3745-13, “A”
(1425) Buenos Aires
Argentina

Posadas 1477-13
(1011) Buenos Aires
Argentina

Maria Siquier  

As a therapeutic method, psychoanalysis provides one of the means for working through traumatic situations stemming from social conditions. Other modalities of elaboration of traumatic situations may exist through many forms of social activity. At least theoretically, however, the psychoanalytic method implies the possibility of integrating the individual's disruptive and reparatory aspects so as to diminish the risk of becoming trapped in an owner-slave, submitter-submitted, sadistic-masochistic dialectic. In this paper we attempt to offer certain ideas on how psychoanalysis as a science can help illuminate two types of social phenomena: some as evident and disruptive as genocide (Nazism, National Reorganization Process in Argentina, 1976-83), others more covert and permanent, such as authoritarianism and its derivatives, which, though less dramatic, may provide the necessary conditions for the former.

Using psychoanalytic theories that refer to ethics as our exploratory starting point, we analyze some of the ways in which human groups sustain their identity in the face of disruptive social conditions.

Dr. Faigon and Dr. Siquier are Training Members of the Buenos Aires Psychoanalytic Association.

Prologue

Donald Ross Issue Co-Editor

Donald Ross

Donald Ross  

The phenomenon of multiple personality disorder (MPD) recently has come upon us like Halley's comet. Absent or hidden for scores of years, it now burns brightly in the diagnostic sky. We are discovering it anew, and with it have come challenges to our conceptualization of psychopathology and the treatment process. Interestingly, not everyone sees it. Even those that do often describe it differently. This secondary phenomenon, the split between MPD experts and skeptics, also deserves our attention and study.

This issue of Inquiry evolved out of a symposium titled, “Viewpoints on Multiple Personality Disorder,” which was held as the 25th Annual Scientific Day program of the Sheppard and Enoch Pratt Hospital on April 21, 1990. An in-depth presentation of a case of MPD by Dr. Kathleen Lyon was followed by a discussion of the case by four experienced clinicians, each with a different viewpoint. The discussion that developed was spirited and stimulating. The case and the discussions by Drs. Putnam, Roth, Ross, and Kluft constitute the main body of this monograph.

One of the problems that became apparent during the symposium was that this was a particularly complicated case. The patient was more than usually difficult and complex, Dr. Lyon was relatively new to the treatment of MPD, the hospital course was prolonged, members of the treatment milieu were seriously split as to their views of MPD, and Dr. Lyon had to transfer the case owing to reality factors outside the scope of therapeutic considerations.
